edition.title: Back to School
edition.coverAlt: Journalmus No. 1, September — Back to School
edition.subtitle: A new year of experiences, discoveries, and good stories.

children.text: Hello, dear readers! It’s, alas, time to go back to school, and that means it’s also time for Parismus to get back to business. This year, we have lots of things planned for you, so don’t forget to follow us! Whether you are an exchange student or a local, Parismus always has a few surprises in store for you. We can’t wait to start this new year full of experiences. Going back to school is never easy, but we can assure you that it can be fun!
In this short but sweet edition, we’ll introduce you to our lovely association, tell you all about this month’s events, and, of course, share some recommendations that might come in handy!
We hope you enjoy reading, and we’ll see you next month for another edition!
Narmin

articles.title: Who Are We?
articles.subtitle: Meet the association bringing students together in Paris.
articles.author: Narmin
articles.excerpt: Parismus began as a way to help Sorbonne students on Erasmus exchanges and grew into a welcoming community for students discovering life in Paris.
articles.imageAlt: Students meeting at a Parismus gathering

children.text: Parismus was created 20 years ago. Its main purpose wasn’t what we might expect today: it wasn’t originally created to help exchange students integrate into Paris. Instead, it was mainly created to help Sorbonne students go on Erasmus exchanges and study abroad.

Over time, however, things went both ways, and Parismus became an important resource for Erasmus students looking to integrate into life in Paris. Through the events Parismus organizes, we are able to help students not only integrate, but also meet new people, discover Paris, go on fun and affordable trips around the country, and, of course, have direct contact with Sorbonne University if they have any questions or issues related to their Erasmus experience.
Parismus is a safe and welcoming space, and every year, the Parismus team works really hard to make all of this happen. We are very happy to be part of it.

articles.title: Events of the Month
articles.subtitle: Three walks through Paris and an Aperismus to start the year together.
articles.author: Narmin
articles.excerpt: Join the Culture Team for the Latin Quarter Walk on September 12, Montmartre on September 19, Belleville on September 26, and Aperismus on September 17.

children.text: This month, we have some events you definitely don’t want to miss! If you’re interested in discovering the city, meeting new people, or simply going for a walk, don’t miss the Latin Quarter Walk on September 12, the Montmartre Walk on September 19, or the Belleville Walk on September 26. The Culture Team has prepared an itinerary to help you discover these beautiful neighborhoods.
And of course, when we say Parismus, we say Aperismus! So don’t miss our first Aperismus of the month on September 17.
Parismus can’t wait to see you all there, so save the dates!

articles.title: Martin Luther King Park
articles.subtitle: A green refuge in the 17th arrondissement, between water, paths, and open space.
articles.author: My Linh
articles.excerpt: A personal guide to one of the places that makes Paris feel spacious, calm, and full of possibility.
articles.imageAlt: Green paths, water, and modern buildings at Martin Luther King Park

children.text: The places we hang out in are a piece of who we are. Paris is never lived the same way for everyone. My childhood living here has nourished parts of who I am, but my walks alone are also waiting for my job to start. Therefore, after 20 years in Paris I think I can share two places that belong in my heart and need to be discovered.

After being two years in the Malesherbes campus in the 17th district and while working in this district, I learned how to love it and cherish it. The 17th has a lot of beautiful places to offer, but today I won’t share the tale of the Monceau Park. Not far from it, by a ten minutes walk, you can find the Martin Luther King Park which also goes a long way till the 18th district. It’s a breeze of fresh air in the middle of the new constructed buildings.

The Park offers a lot of facilities; it’s perfect for all types of activities, there is a skate park, a basketball field, and places where you could play tennis. The Park is one of the biggest in Paris and facilities such as kids’ play areas are placed all among the Park.

It’s the catch, if you are a runner searching for a beautiful place surrounded by water, sand, and wonderful bridges. And how could I forget the many picnics? Here, there’s no need to fight to have a piece of grass with a bit of privacy without being glued to the others. The park is big enough to accommodate a large number of people no matter what time! It really feels like not being in Paris.

And finally, the park also has its own café/food court/bar, the latter is called HOBA. It has a terrace where the food court is located and a low terrace near a water corner where the café/bar is located! It is ideal to recharge your batteries and share a good time with loved ones. Now that you know where to take refuge in the 17th arrondissement, you won’t miss any more space for your picnics!

articles.title: The Nightingale — Kristin Hannah
articles.subtitle: Two sisters, occupied France, and the quiet heroism of resistance.
articles.author: Sofia
articles.excerpt: Kristin Hannah’s novel follows Vianne and Isabelle as they face impossible choices in occupied France during the Second World War.
articles.imageAlt: The Nightingale by Kristin Hannah book cover

children.text: In The Nightingale, Kristin Hannah transports her readers to occupied France in 1940 through the lives of two sisters who could not be more different: Vianne, who struggles to protect her daughter and her home under Nazi occupation, and Isabelle, a passionate and rebellious young woman who joins the Resistance. As the war disrupts their everyday lives, each sister is forced to face impossible choices, embodying two different forms of female courage in the face of the horrors of the time.

This poignant story sheds light on the unspeakable trauma of the Second World War, from roundups to summary executions, while celebrating the quiet heroism of ordinary women who risked their lives to save Allied airmen and Jewish children.

It is a vivid portrait of a time when every act of solidarity became an act of survival and defiance against oppression. Ultimately, this novel explores the tragic human condition, where every choice becomes a moral compass between submission, which offers protection, and rebellion, which may lead to condemnation. The Nightingale reveals that it is through selflessness in the face of nothingness that humanity finds its highest dignity.

articles.title: Fontaines D.C. Make Their Comeback with “Marianne”
articles.subtitle: A new single opens the door to the band’s next chapter.
articles.author: Raquel
articles.excerpt: The Irish post-punk band returns with an introspective single about escapism, pleasure, and the pull of another world.
articles.imageAlt: Fontaines D.C. band portrait and Dopamine Chamber artwork

children.text: The Irish post-punk sensation Fontaines D.C. has just made a major impact on the music scene. On August 18, the band unveiled “Marianne,” a bold new single that serves as a launchpad for their highly anticipated fifth studio album, Dopamine Chamber, which is set for worldwide release on October 16.

“Marianne” is much more than a simple alternative rock track; it is an introspective piece accompanied by a visually hallucinatory music video directed by Dave Meyers. The song turns escapism and the relentless pursuit of pleasure into a way of breaking free from a reality marked by catastrophe. Through its poignant lyrics, the song explores the possibility of disappearing, whether through physically escaping to an idealized elsewhere or through deliberately surrendering to hedonism.

Charismatic frontman Grian Chatten directly invites the listener to follow him and leave the real world behind. Beneath this invitation to let go, however, lies a deeper existential conflict: the constant tension between the vital need to take refuge in fantasy and the burden of remaining conscious in an increasingly difficult and overwhelming era.

To understand the significance of this new chapter, it is worth looking back at Fontaines D.C.’s meteoric rise. Formed in Dublin in 2017 by five friends who were students at BIMM (British and Irish Modern Music Institute), the quintet is made up of Grian Chatten (vocals), Carlos O’Connell (guitar), Conor Curley (guitar), Conor Deegan III (bass), and Tom Coll (drums). Sharing a common love of urban literature, the Grammy-nominated band broke through in 2019 with Dogrel, a raw debut album that received widespread critical acclaim. They then cemented their status with A Hero’s Death (2020), an album steeped in disillusionment, followed by Skinty Fia (2022), which explored their Irish heritage, before taking a new direction with the excellent Romance in 2024.

The Dopamine Chamber era is sure to make itself heard everywhere. After previewing “Marianne” and other unreleased tracks at recent summer festivals, the band will soon embark on a massive world tour. It will be the perfect opportunity for audiences to dive headfirst into the live, cathartic world of one of the most essential modern rock bands of our time.
